D009-D008_h020.question_both: I’ve been feeling… off… for the past few months. The low times started around last winter—just after the supply boat left. It hit me slowly: I’d sit in the lantern room for hours, staring at the beam sweep the cliffs, but not really seeing it. No music, no reading, not even the radio held my attention. Just this hollow feeling, like I’d been emptied out. I kept thinking I’d done something wrong—I once convinced myself that forgetting to log a weather note had put ships at risk. That thought looped for days. About two months ago, it shifted. I can’t say I felt better, but I started cleaning every bolt and pane in the tower, repainting the stair rails, fixing the generator even when it worked fine. I’d start three things at once—rewiring the light panel, drafting letters I’d never send, pacing the gallery for hours. My mind jumps now, can’t settle. I snapped at the relief ranger last week over nothing. But I’m still making the rounds, still keeping the light going. The low days are longer, deeper—they’ve got me thinking about how easy it’d be to just… not climb back down after a shift up top. I’ve pictured it too clearly. But no, I haven’t told anyone.
D009-D008_h020.question_a:
I’ve been the keeper at this remote lighthouse for eight years now—quiet work, just me and the rhythm of the tide. About four months ago, I started feeling… hollow. Like the fog outside had seeped into my chest. I stopped fixing the old radio I used to tinker with. Didn’t care to read, didn’t even notice the sunrise—something I used to love. I kept thinking I’d failed somehow—like if I’d just been better, more careful, my dad wouldn’t have gotten sick. I even figured out how I’d step into the sea on a foggy night when no one could see. It felt like the only way to make it right.

But then, three weeks ago, something shifted. Not better—different. I wasn’t sad anymore, just restless. I repainted the whole tower in a weekend, rewired the backup generator, started planning a signal upgrade that’s way beyond my budget. I snapped at the supply pilot for being ten minutes late—little things set me off. My brain jumps from one idea to the next, never settles. I can’t focus long enough to finish a thought.

But I never lost touch with reality, and I didn’t need to be hospitalized. Just… swung from dead inside to wired for no good reason.
D009-D008_h020.question_b:
I’ve been the keeper here at the lighthouse for twelve years now—quiet work, just how I like it. But about four months ago, everything started to change. At first, I thought it was just a rough patch. I stopped caring about things I used to enjoy, like fixing old radios or watching the stars. Just felt... empty, like there was a hole inside. I couldn’t focus on anything—even a book or the radio news. I kept thinking I’d failed in small things: forgetting to log a weather report, missing a routine check—and I’d sit there convinced I deserved to be punished for it. I even started planning how I’d end it, down to the time and place.

But before that, there was a strange stretch—about three weeks—where I couldn’t sit still. I repainted the whole tower, rewired the generator, started rebuilding the dock for no reason. I snapped at the supply boat guy over nothing. Couldn’t focus on one task—started ten at once. But I didn’t think it was a problem then.  

The low, though—this depression—it’s crippling. I can’t do my job properly. I had to radio for help once during a storm because I couldn’t bring myself to climb the stairs. That’s never happened before.

It wasn’t rage, but I had zero patience.

That passed, and then everything just… slowed. For over a year, I’ve felt heavy. Even picking up my pencil to sketch a wireframe feels effortful. I don’t enjoy my work anymore—nothing makes me happy. My husband says I take forever to answer simple questions. I just can’t think straight; my brain gets tired so fast, even reading a design brief. Some days, I sit at my desk for hours and barely ship anything. I’m not suicidal, but I do wonder if I’ll ever feel like myself again.

The key thing? When I was high, I wasn’t psychotic, and I still delivered work—so no hospitalization. But the depression has cost me—it’s ruined deadlines, strained my marriage. That’s why I’m here.
